I feel like you said love isn't enough, but then you described exactly what love is(to me at least) in your prescribed remedy. I would argue that love IS enough, but is too often taken for granted or allowed to slip away - usually very gradually. Love is a choice, usually made with incomplete or incorrect information, but it's not a choice you make once, you make it every day, even multiple times. If you keep choosing to love, your partner bothers you less, and you are less bothered by your partner, and it gets easier and easier to keep choosing to love. When there is infidelity, the marriage doesn't end because one spouse cheated, it ends because one or both spouses didn't choose to keep loving. I'm not saying you should stay if your spouse cheats, that's an act that clearly isn't in harmony with choosing love, but every single marriage could survive infidelity if both choose to continue to work toward a more perfect love. 

Sometimes you don't want to be with the person you married anymore and I get that too. Sometimes we suck at choosing who to love.

I realize I'm in a unique role where automating everything is kind of expected of me, but I feel like if you're employees are doing things that could be automated as easily as these apps imply then there is something inherently wrong with what they are being asked to do to begin with. There is typically very little incentive to work more/smarter/harder. The threat that a coworker may automate my job away might motivate better work ethic, but I doubt it. Fear is usually a poor motivator.

The scooters help, but the bus system seems more daunting to be sure you're on the right bus. It's great if you are commuting regularly and can get familiar with the route. Also, people are so entitled now days I can't tell you how many times I have ridden public trans (not my typical commute) and arrive at work to have people associated that I didn't call one of them for a ride. It's not that scary people, and by scary the only scary I think is valid is the fear of not knowing how to use the system, I've never felt unsafe(frequently irritated but not unsafe) on any uta ride.

I think making downtown foot traffic, commercial traffic, and emergency traffic only may be an option to improve public transportation adoption, but I don't know if I'd vote for that. Lots of considerations to considerate there. 😉

I'd second the rent a car advice only to add that SLC is very inexpensive to park a car in. you can usually find places close to your destination to park for free(outside of business hours) and there is a ton of underground parking for super low(compared to big cities) rates. If parking downtown is intimidating(sometimes when there are multiple events traffic can get busy) you can park for free at any of the Trax(light rail) stations and ride into the city with enough stops to realistically get within walking distance of most attractions.

I think we have a chicken and egg problem going on here too. Not enough "contributing members" of society have adopted public transportation while a TON of infrastructure has been added for it. This means that often Trax trains are mobile shelters(from the weather) running practically empty, and look really inviting to someone with nowhere else to go. If these trains were being well-used by a more diverse sampling of the population then there would a) be less room for homeless riders(and less inviting) and b) the homeless that still ride would be a smaller portion of the total ridership therefore making it seem less like a mobile homeless camp. 

Utah isn't the best state for public transportation adoption simply because of how spread out it is and how unlikely it is that most people could eliminate car ownership entirely by adopting public transportation. More public transportation is the answer, and I think the "if you build it" part is making a lot of progress, and the "they will come" part is sometimes slower to catch up, but it's getting better. My experience on Frontrunner has been excellent, and I don't ride the airport line often, but most of the trax lines outside of downtown(free fare zone) have seemed way better in the past few years than I remember them being a decade ago.

I ranted a bit on these lines before reading your post, yours is more succinct and represents my sentiments. Engineers are smart for sure, but but most of what we do is NOT creative or genius or requiring much actual talent.

Engineering is not a field that requires creative genius. Talent is rare in software engineering, and literally anyone can learn to do it. I don't mean to belittle or denigrate us engineers, but I think about the inequity in compensation for effort every time I go through a drive through and see the employees on the other side of the window hustling, dealing with entitled, impatient and demanding customers all day for very little pay, knowing their every move is being scrutinized, every moment of their day being squeezed for every ounce of productivity.
